# Heartland AI Campus — Alberta development proposal

**Concept / pre-feasibility edition · 13 October 2026 · all monetary amounts CAD unless stated**

**Decision: the base case fails the 15% return hurdle. Advance only a bounded program to validate site, power, achievable rent and cost; do not take an investment decision.** The proposal is a complete development concept for a 100 MW IT campus in Strathcona County, delivered in four 25 MW phases. It is not an application, engineered design, valuation, offer to lease, investment solicitation or representation that the identified property is available.

The asset business is a landlord/operator supplying powered, cooled and connected IT capacity. The tenant buys and operates GPUs and other IT equipment. The model includes facility and proposed generation capital; it excludes GPU/cloud revenue and does not use that revenue to make the property economics work. No landowner, regulator, utility, vendor, customer or lender has been contacted for this study.

## Investment proposition and present weakness

A large industrial-area site with new modular generation can support a technically credible Alberta development. The commercial proposition is four separately commissioned buildings, a shared but sectionalized utility backbone, liquid cooling and dry heat rejection, a clearly documented power operating envelope, and expansion rights that turn into construction commitments only when the tenant and financing support them.

The distinction between an attractive Alberta narrative and an executable project is substantial. The initial AESO 1,200 MW large-load allocation is fully assigned; this project holds no allocation. AESO's latest dated BYOG update inspected, September 8, 2026, says final materials were still being completed and intake was expected in fall. That evidence supports developing a BYOG application; it does not support promising access, a qualifying generator ratio, bridging load or a service date. [AB02](https://www.aeso.ca/grid/connecting-to-the-grid/large-load-projects/)[AB03](https://aesoengage.aeso.ca/pre-engagement-phase-ii-large-load-integration)

The chosen site is a real marketed tract, but its listing identifies agricultural zoning. Nearby transmission, a gas franchise and an estimated fibre flag are leads to investigate, not deliverable services. The strongest first product for a prospective partner is therefore a bounded development package with explicit failure tests, not a claim of shovel-ready capacity. [AB01](https://regionaldashboard.alberta.ca/property/201504)

## 1. Site selection and control strategy

**Working candidate:** the marketed 160-acre tract at Township Road 564 and Range Road 211, Strathcona County; legal description **SE 23-56-21-W4**. The provincial dashboard places it in the Sandhills Heavy Industrial Policy Area and gives a listing map pin at **53.866399, -113.001632**. The full listing HTML contains that coordinate; it is not a survey coordinate or proof of property boundaries. **160 acres converts to approximately 64.75 hectares.** [AB01](https://regionaldashboard.alberta.ca/property/201504)

[Open the candidate location](https://www.openstreetmap.org/?mlat=53.866399&mlon=-113.001632#map=13/53.866399/-113.001632)

The same public record reports a nearby AltaLink 240 kV corridor. Geographic proximity warrants a connection study, but does not settle thermal capacity, system stability, access rights, line tapping, route feasibility or cost. The listing's fibre indicator is estimated. Current asking price, seller willingness, title, availability and occupation were not established. All engineering diagrams are conceptual arrangements, never a surveyed overlay. [AB01](https://regionaldashboard.alberta.ca/property/201504)

### Land program

Seek a conditional, assignable option over the whole tract, with access for investigations, staged option payments, extension rights tied to public approvals, and exit rights for power, gas, environmental, geotechnical, zoning and customer failures. Obtain title/caveats, legal and beneficial owner confirmation, mortgages, surface/mineral rights, utility and pipeline easements, access rights and property-tax history. Do not purchase speculatively on the strength of the website listing.

Use a **600 m × 800 m campus envelope, 48 ha**, plus an adjoining **187.5 m × 800 m generation zone, 15 ha**: a **787.5 m × 800 m combined envelope, 63 ha gross** within the listed 64.75 ha tract. Only approximately 1.75 ha remains unallocated, so the site fit is tight and must be tested against the actual boundaries, easements and hazards. The campus envelope includes conceptual drainage and buffers; none is a finding of usable land. Indicative footprint allocation is:

| Component | Planning allocation | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|
| Four hall shells | 8.64 ha | Four nominal 180 m × 120 m buildings, 25 MW IT each |
| Facility electrical and cooling yards | 12 ha | Modular services, acoustic separation, maintenance access |
| Gas plant, engine cooling, exhaust and BESS | 15 ha outside campus envelope | Separate plant safety and operating zone |
| Grid receiving station | 3 ha | Concept four-transformer station and service corridors |
| Roads, loading, security and parking | 7 ha | Fire circulation, replacement-equipment routes and construction access |
| Campus drainage, buffers and reserved space | 17.36 ha | Preliminary balance within the 48 ha campus; must expand if field constraints require it |

No setbacks in this allocation are statutory claims. A local planner, surveyor, civil engineer and fire authority must determine the permitted arrangement. Buildings should remain separate from the plant acoustic boundary and industrial-neighbour hazard contours. Reserve two independent fibre entries and prevent their construction paths from converging at a single culvert or bridge.

The AG listing and the County's distinction between AG, IHH, IMH and utility zones require written use classification and a mapped zoning check. A heavy-industrial *policy* area does not substitute for the applicable zone or development permit. [AB06](https://www.strathcona.ca/council-county/bylaws-and-policies/land-use-bylaw/interactive-lub/part-1-interpretation/zones-and-maps/)

## 2. Power: selected route and rejected shortcuts

The base concept is **new generation paired with a conditional transmission connection**, with an island-capable design pursued only if studies, approvals, fuel security and customer terms support it. Alberta policy directs data centres toward new supply and cost responsibility for upgrades; that means generation and connection costs must be visible in the project. [AB05](https://www.alberta.ca/powering-new-pathways-for-data-centres)

| Operating quantity | Concept value | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Ultimate IT nameplate | 100 MW | Four blocks of 25 MW; rentable IT boundary |
| Annual PUE target | 1.20 | Energy ratio at stated operating assumptions, not a peak guarantee |
| Peak facility envelope | 125 MW | 1.25 × IT; sizing allowance pending equipment guarantees |
| Proposed generation | 160 MW net at site | 16 procurement modules targeting 10 MW net each |
| With two modules unavailable | 140 MW | Arithmetic headroom above 125 MW; not a reliability certification |
| Plant-side storage | 25 MW / 25 MWh | Initial dynamic-support allowance, subject to simulation |
| Grid receiving concept | 240/34.5 kV; 4 × 50 MVA | Three duty plus one spare; station within facility electrical cost; connection not selected |

The gas modules are installed in cumulative stages of **6 / 9 / 13 / 16** for **25 / 50 / 75 / 100 MW IT**. Physical additions remain **6 / 3 / 4 / 3 engines**, but generation **cost** shares are **47.0486% / 15.8854% / 21.1806% / 15.8854%**. The CAD25m gas lateral and CAD30m BESS are fully funded in phase 1; the other CAD305m follows incremental module counts. This gives phase plant hard costs of **CAD169.375m / CAD57.1875m / CAD76.25m / CAD57.1875m**. Remaining balance-of-plant and civils are allocated proportionally as an approximation; actual deposits and cancellation liabilities are not modeled. At the first stage, four available modules after two outages give 40 MW against a 31.25 MW facility envelope. At later stages that comparison is 70 versus 62.5 MW, 110 versus 93.75 MW, and 140 versus 125 MW. These balances assume **net guaranteed site capacity**, not catalogue rating, and do not prove transient stability or fuel availability.

Manufacturer data demonstrates an appropriate engine size class; published reference performance must be derated for the actual site, auxiliaries, gas and emissions requirements. The independent concept assumes **7.6 GJ/MWh net heat rate**. It does not select a manufacturer or reserve a factory slot. [AB11](https://www.wartsila.com/energy/engine-power-plant-solutions/engine-power-plant-products/wartsila-31sg-gas-engine)

### Alternatives to the selected power route

1. **Grid-only campus:** do not use as the base case without a new allocation and binding service terms. A line nearby does not resolve the large-load process.
2. **Remote generator partnership / eligible paired supply:** retain as a commercial alternative if it offers a cheaper bankable delivery path. It requires the same discipline on eligibility, transmission, risk allocation and net cost. If a partner owns the plant, remove plant CAPEX only while adding the full power/capacity-payment obligation; never remove both.
3. **Fully off-grid operation:** retain as a separately approved fallback, not a shortcut around power-plant, environmental or municipal approvals. Its gas-supply common-mode failure, island dynamics, black-start and tenant SLA requirements are more demanding.
4. **Renewables-plus-storage:** evaluate as emissions and energy-price diversification, without assuming a firm 125 MW round-the-clock obligation is satisfied by annual energy matching. No renewable or export revenues support the base case.

### Grid and controls package

Commission the load and generator study together: staged maximum demand, step and cyclic loads, fault ride-through, harmonics, reactive requirements, grounding, protection discrimination, loss of mains, controlled islanding and reconnection. Identify the exact applicable AESO and reliability obligations through the connection process. The AESO technical guide discusses possible 10 MW/min point-of-connection ramp limits and coordination requirements; this is a design prompt, not an approved site-specific operating limit. [AB04](https://www.aeso.ca/assets/Uploads/grid/Guide-to-AESO-Connection-Requirements-for-Transmission-Connected-Data-Centres.pdf)

A plant BESS may smooth ramps and support an island, but **25 MW cannot absorb or supply a full 125 MW instantaneous imbalance**. The controller must coordinate engine reserve, UPS, load modulation and protective shedding. A 25 MWh energy rating alone does not establish ride-through. The integrated test plan must demonstrate the actual largest credible disturbance and all allowed transitions.

Four transformers arranged N+1 do not prove independent utility supplies. Require the transmission owner to disclose upstream common elements and permitted import/export under outages. Similarly, N+2 engines sharing one gas main do not create diverse fuel. Independent facility emergency supply and full-path UPS remain in the facility scope until a customer-approved reliability analysis allows a different configuration.

### Gas and emissions

The working peak gas reservation is **0.8 million standard m³/day**. It is derived from 160 MW × 7.6 GJ/MWh × 24 hours divided by an assumed 38 MJ/m³ gas energy content, rounded upward. At 125 MW actual plant output the corresponding quantity is approximately 0.60 million m³/day. Require a firm delivery and pressure study, maximum-day rights, actual gas assay, curtailment history, upstream outage map, metering/regulation redundancy and lateral easements. A local gas franchise boundary is not a high-pressure industrial service contract.

At 95% committed occupancy and 80% load on committed IT, the campus averages 76 MW IT. At PUE 1.20 it consumes about **799 GWh/year** at the facility electrical boundary. If that entire supply were generated by the assumed engines, a screening factor of 0.38 tCO2/MWh gives roughly **304,000 tonnes of direct CO2 annually**, excluding upstream emissions and methane slip. This is a scenario calculation, not an inventory, guaranteed dispatch pattern or low-carbon claim.

TIER treatment must be developed as a benchmark-based compliance case. The provincial guidance generally covers emitters above 100,000 tonnes CO2e/year and describes benchmark-based obligations. Do not multiply gross emissions by a headline tax and call it the statutory liability. [AB10](https://www.alberta.ca/technology-innovation-and-emissions-reduction-regulation) The May 2026 Canada–Alberta agreement conditionally holds the federal Clean Electricity Regulations in abeyance during litigation; it does not establish a permanent exemption for this plant. Finance counsel must support the operating and emissions path over the financing term. [AB16](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/backgrounders/2026/05/15/implementation-agreement-canada-alberta-memorandum-understanding)

## 3. Cooling, water and engineering interfaces

The target product is dense liquid-cooled capacity, with a starting equivalent of **1,000 racks at 100 kW/rack**. This is a capacity equivalence, not a confirmed server layout. Confirm the tenant's liquid fraction, inlet/outlet temperatures, water chemistry, connector type, pressure, allowable transients and responsibility at the CDU. Do not order cooling hardware around an unspecified GPU generation.

Use separate technology-cooling and facility loops, redundant CDUs/pumps and outdoor freeze-protected glycol circuits. Plan a 10 K facility-loop temperature difference for initial hydraulic sizing, subject to customer requirements. As a dimensional check, 100 MW transferred to water at 10 K requires approximately **2.39 m³/s** using 4.18 kJ/kg-K and 1,000 kg/m³; 25 MW is about 0.60 m³/s. Glycol reduces heat capacity and changes pump duty, so this is not a pipe-sizing result. Dual loops, redundancy and design margin increase installed equipment capacity.

The model assigns **90 MW to liquid capture and 10 MW to residual IT air cooling**, with a conservative **125 MW aggregate campus heat-rejection envelope** including peak facility overhead. At the stated 4.186 kJ/kg-K and 997 kg/m³ water assumptions, the 90 MW / 10 K liquid circuit circulates approximately 7,763 m³/hour. Final equipment sizing must locate compressor/fan/pump heat and electrical losses within the actual loops; the 125 MW aggregate is not one mandatory water loop. The gas plant has **separate engine jacket-water, charge-air and exhaust heat systems**; 160 MW electrical generation is not a 160 MW thermal load, and the campus dry-cooler figure cannot cover the engine plant.

Use dry heat rejection with mechanical trim for high ambient temperatures, not evaporative cooling towers in the base design. **+35°C summer design check, +40°C stress check and −40°C winter check are explicit project assumptions**, not sourced design statistics. Obtain hourly dry-bulb/wet-bulb data and appropriate code design values before guaranteeing PUE or capacity. The ECCC climate-normal service is the official starting point, but no site-hourly simulation was performed here. [AB12](https://www.climate.weather.gc.ca/climate_normals/index_e.html)

Winterization must include glycol concentration, separation of indoor water from exposed circuits, idle-equipment freeze risk, restart controls, snow and ice access, heated critical enclosures, drainback and pipe movement. Smoke and dust require filter strategy and differential-pressure monitoring. Redundant mechanical trains must retain maintainability when one train is unavailable at the design envelope.

**Zero routine evaporative cooling is an engineering intent, not zero water use.** Plan domestic/service supply initially at 50 m³/day, with first fill, maintenance disposal and fire demand separately assessed. Size fire storage and replenishment against the local fire analysis; do not invent a municipal hydrant capacity. Wetlands, drainage changes, construction water and wastewater can require authorization even with dry cooling. [AB09](https://www.alberta.ca/water-legislation-and-guidelines)

Other deliverables before detailed design are a frost/geotechnical foundation design, stormwater retention and release plan, flood and surface-drainage review, hazardous-neighbour screening, fire vehicle/access design, battery/UPS fire strategy, fuel-spill containment, security zoning and two-carrier route diversity evidence.

## 4. Permitting and approvals sequence

This proposal separates municipal permission for the campus from permission for its power facilities. AUC Rule 007 provides current facility application requirements and forms for the relevant generation and electrical infrastructure; AUC guidance also identifies separate environmental and noise obligations. [AB07](https://www.auc.ab.ca/rules/rule007/)[AB08](https://www.auc.ab.ca/proposing-a-power-plant-application/) The exact regulatory boundaries and applicable current law must be confirmed for the final configuration.

| Workstream | Indicative sequence | Approval evidence required before release |
|---|---|---|
| Land and title | M1–6 | Conditional control, survey, easements, investigation rights |
| County classification / rezoning / development | M2–18 | Written use interpretation, applicable zoning/development consents and conditions |
| AESO / transmission-owner process | M2–36 assumption | Final-route eligibility, completed studies, agreements, contributions and operating envelope |
| AUC generation and electrical facilities | M5–24 | Relevant approvals following required application and engagement process |
| Air/environment and noise | M4–24 | Applicable EPEA approvals, dispersion/noise outcomes and operating conditions |
| Water/wetlands/drainage | M3–20 | Activity/diversion approvals where needed, supply and discharge arrangements |
| Indigenous / participant involvement | Begin M2; through approval | Applicable consultation determination, process completion and documented responses |
| Gas lateral and roads | M3–36 | Supplier and regulator approvals, easements and transport/access permits |
| Building and safety codes | M14–42, then by phase | Building/trade/pressure/fire compliance and occupancy evidence |
| Tax and operating compliance | Resolve before finance close | Levy payer/rate treatment, TIER/other reporting and operating register |

These month ranges are scheduling assumptions, not regulator service standards. Hearings, consultation, environmental field seasons, route objections and incomplete applications can extend them. Do not underwrite an expedited-approval entitlement or a waived assessment. Begin engagement with nearby land users and potentially affected Indigenous communities early; neither a private-land option nor an industrial policy designation proves consent.

## 5. Delivery and procurement plan

**Month 1 is the authorized start of actual development, not today's date.** The base scenario accepts 25 / 50 / 75 / 100 MW at **M42 / M51 / M60 / M69**. It is not an AESO energization forecast. The full month-by-month workstream schedule is in `monthly-schedule.csv`.

The critical path is the latest of (a) land-use/environment/power consents, (b) firm fuel and grid service, (c) manufacture and transport of engines/transformers/switchgear, and (d) construction plus witnessed integrated testing. Hall construction by itself cannot pull that date forward.

| Period | Deliverable and decision |
|---|---|
| M1–3 | Site/control screening, title and services map, first fatal-flaw review |
| M2–8 | Provider feasibility, tenant design brief and scoped technical applications |
| M3–6 | Conditional land option and G0 decision; reject the tract if fundamental constraints fail |
| M6–12 | Anchor terms, power/fuel route and budget validation; explicit stop/continue decision |
| M8–38 | Conditional long-lead reservations, engineering and manufacture, with funded cancellation exposure |
| M12–24 | Commercial/FID work, consents and detailed design; conditions must actually be met before irreversible releases |
| M20–34 | Shared civil works and first shell, released only with required approvals |
| M30–42 | Initial 60 MW gas stage and first 25 MW IT fit-out; protection, thermal and operational tests |
| M36–51 | Block 2 and generation expansion to 90 MW cumulative |
| M45–60 | Block 3 and generation expansion to 130 MW cumulative |
| M54–69 | Block 4 and generation expansion to 160 MW cumulative |

The aggressive M42 first-phase scenario **depends on equity-funded conditional equipment reservations / limited notices starting around M8**. A 30-month long-lead package then arrives around M38. Those commitments can precede final permits and must carry explicitly approved cancellation exposure; they are not authorized purchases in this artifact. If orders wait until later approvals, move service dates later and rerun the model. Do not preserve the attractive schedule while removing the early-order risk.

Tender equipment and EPC scope through packages with clear interfaces: receiving station; gas lateral; modular engines/BOP; plant BESS/controls; civil/shell; facility electrical/UPS/emergency supply; cooling/CDUs; carriers; integrated controls; and independent commissioning. Planning lead allowances are 30 months for major station equipment and engines, 24 months for gas infrastructure, 18–20 months for major facility systems, and 15 months for diverse fibre work. None is a vendor commitment.

Every major package requires a bid comparison with exclusions, currency, incoterms/delivery point, tax, guarantee conditions, spare parts, escalation, delay damages, warranty, termination rights and service support. Separate factory tests from installation acceptance and integrated performance tests. Require the OEM's net output/heat-rate/noise/emissions guarantees at agreed site conditions; catalogue gross performance cannot satisfy the acceptance schedule.

The independent commissioning authority should own a failure matrix including utility loss, transformer/MV section loss, engine and gas-system trips, BESS unavailability, cooling train/pump loss, communications loss, smoke filtration, UPS bypass and controlled restoration. Customer service starts only after witnessed tests, permits, operating procedures, trained staff and formal acceptance. Concurrent maintenance is a design target, not a Tier certification or a promise of fault tolerance.

## 6. Commercial model and customer qualification

The anchor product is a dedicated 25 MW building divided into five 5 MW suites, with paid expansion options over later buildings. Target a 10–15 year take-or-pay capacity lease supported by a parent guarantee or letter of credit. The tenant's credit and delivery obligations matter more than an impressive company name in a prospect list; no prospect interest is assumed. The 20-year operating model assumes continued occupancy after the proposed 10–15 year initial lease expires. A 15-year initial lease leaves five modeled operating years uncontracted for phase 1, and approximately 2.75 for phase 4 under this horizon. No renewal downtime, inducement, rent haircut or tenant-capital replacement is modeled. That tail requires a renewal/reletting downside and cannot be presented to lenders as signed revenue.

The contract must separate:

- Committed IT kW, minimum rent and reservation fees from actual metered IT energy.
- Capacity rent from pass-through energy operating costs and the operating-risk sharing mechanism.
- Landlord facility availability from tenant software/GPU availability.
- Normal maintenance and regulator-directed curtailment from avoidable landlord failure.
- Generation capital recovery from gas, service, carbon and balancing costs.
- Landlord property obligations from the computing-equipment levy and other tenant-specific taxes.
- Capacity acceptance tests from cloud benchmark tests outside the landlord's scope.

Alberta's tax overview states that a levy on large data-centre computing equipment became effective January 1, 2026, with rates up to 2% and lower rates associated with own-power solutions. **GPU exclusion from this model does not establish an exemption.** Tax counsel must identify the legally liable entity, reporting boundary, actual rate and any credit treatment; the lease needs an enforceable reimbursement mechanism where appropriate. No levy saving or tax credit is capitalized in the base facility value. [AB15](https://www.alberta.ca/taxes-levies-overview)

The go-to-market package is a design brief, constraint map, power-service case, programme, delivered-cost schedule and draft interface/acceptance requirements. Qualify Canadian data-residency requirements, emissions policy, permitted workloads, peak step behavior, density, temperatures, fibre latency and willingness to accept the actual AESO operating envelope. A tenant that requires an incompatible emissions or uptime product is not a fit even at an attractive headline rent.

## 7. Native-CAD underwriting and cost boundary

All numbers below are **independent screening estimates**, not current vendor quotes, comparable transactions or lender terms. They are designed to expose the cost/rent thresholds that the next diligence phase must validate. Regional assumptions were constructed independently of the Texas proposal.

| Input | Base assumption | Estimation basis |
|---|---:|---|
| Facility hard cost | CAD13,500/kW IT | CAD2,430 shell/fit-out + 5,400 electrical/UPS/standby + 2,970 cooling/CDUs + 1,350 civil/drainage + 675 controls/security/fibre + 675 testing/commissioning |
| Facility hard cost at 100 MW | CAD1,350m | Excludes land, receiving-grid scope, gas generation, soft cost and contingency |
| Land | CAD8m | CAD50,000/acre placeholder for whole tract; seller price not established |
| Off-plot grid interface | CAD75m | External line/route, reinforcement contributions, easements and utility studies; receiving station already in facility electrical; replace with actual study |
| Generation + plant BESS | CAD360m | Engine packages 175m + generation BOP 85m + gas lateral 25m + BESS 30m + dedicated plant civils/electrical 45m |
| Direct subtotal | CAD1,793m | Before soft costs, contingency and model-specific financing treatment |
| Soft cost | 10% of direct | Development, engineering, permitting, legal and owner management |
| Contingency | 15% of hard plus soft cost | Concept reserve; not a probabilistic confidence claim |
| Fixed non-energy OPEX | CAD35m/year ultimate | Facility/plant staffing 8m, property tax 18m, insurance 4m, fixed plant service 2m, security/admin 3m |
| Variable non-energy OPEX | CAD180/committed kW-year | Facility maintenance and consumables; no duplicate gas service cost |
| Capacity rent | CAD235/committed kW-month | Price to test against customer bids; no market quotation represented |
| Stabilized commitment / actual load | 95% / 80% | Distinct rent-bearing capacity and utilization assumptions |
| Senior debt / rate / amortization | 55% / 7.5% / 20 years | Conditional target, not a financing offer |
| Equity hurdle | 15% | Developer screen |

The operating energy allowance is **CAD120/MWh** at the facility boundary: delivered fuel CAD41.8 (7.6 GJ/MWh × CAD5.50/GJ), plant variable service CAD17, emissions reserve CAD25, residual grid/transport/balancing CAD21.2, and operations reserve CAD15. These buckets are scenario allowances and must be replaced by an actual dispatch/tariff/fuel model. The emissions reserve is not a calculated statutory TIER bill. Generation capital is already included above and recovered through rent, so a capital-recovery adder must not also be included here.

At the stabilized assumptions, capacity rent is **CAD267.9m/year** (95,000 kW × CAD235 × 12). Fixed plus variable non-energy costs total **CAD52.1m/year**, before any model-specific additional reserves or deductions. Metered facility energy is approximately **798,912 MWh/year**, costing and reimbursing approximately **CAD95.87m/year** at the assumed rate, with no energy trading margin. These arithmetic checks are not debt service, net profit or an IRR. The interactive model provides the time-dependent investment outputs and its explicit financing/terminal assumptions.

The model applies soft cost to direct cost, then contingency to direct plus soft: CAD1,793m + CAD179.3m + CAD295.845m = **CAD2,268.145m before financing**. Do not silently add an allowance twice or call unfinanced construction cost total equity funding. Debt needs depend on draw timing, capitalized interest/fees, debt-service reserves, and operating carry during phase-up. Tax, depreciation, GST financing/recovery and entity-specific levy incidence require a separate tax/cash model before finance close.

### Current model result and investment decision

The executable base case yields **negative CAD419.26m equity NPV at a 15% hurdle**, with **CAD2,382.25m total modeled funding including CAD114.11m of capitalized interest**. Stabilized EBITDA is CAD215.8m and cash available for debt service after the model maintenance-capital reserve is CAD198.7m. These values are generated from the same assumptions used by the interactive model; the conclusion is **no investment decision at current price and cost assumptions**.

The equity IRR is **undefined as a single investment measure**: the model detects multiple roots, so the displayed IRR must remain unavailable rather than selecting the flattering root. The unlevered IRR is about **5.20%**. Minimum ordinary operating DSCR is approximately **1.27×**, but minimum DSCR **including the terminal repayment is only 0.45×**. A **CAD130.72m debt balloon** remains when the model ends because later-phase 20-year loans extend beyond a horizon measured 20 operating years from the first phase. That is a terminal funding requirement, not ordinary operating default evidence by itself.

The model assigns **zero terminal enterprise/land value**, assumes constant nominal inputs and excludes tax benefits; these choices matter to valuation. A future sale or refinance cannot be treated as committed funding. The capacity rent required to reach zero equity NPV at the chosen 15% hurdle is approximately **CAD339.28/kW-month**, versus the assumed CAD235. That is a calculated threshold to test, **not an assertion that customers will pay it**. An executable case needs demonstrably better cost, price, timing or risk structure, followed by a fresh investment decision.

The fixed OPEX estimate explicitly includes plant staffing and fixed service. The CAD18m property-tax allowance is informed by published 2026 Strathcona rates: approximately CAD900m assumed non-residential assessment and CAD400m assumed machinery/equipment assessment produce roughly CAD18m tax before small additional adjustments. Those assessment values are assumptions, not cost-to-assessment equivalence or a County ruling. No industrial tax incentive is assumed. [AB17](https://www.strathcona.ca/your-property-utilities/property-taxes/tax-payment/tax-rates/)

### Finance and downside discipline

Use a sponsor holding company with facility and generation SPVs, documented easements and a power-service agreement. Consolidate both asset costs for investment evaluation. A partner's separate capital is still an economic cost if recovered in power or capacity payments.

Debt should follow a signed credit-supported anchor lease, service certainty, required permits, firm EPC scope and completion support. The sponsor must fund early diligence and any equipment cancellation risk before lenders are willing to fund. Later blocks require their own tenant and capacity gates; one tenant's non-binding expansion intention cannot secure debt for the full campus.

At minimum, test total cost +35%, capacity rent −20%, occupancy 70%, first service +12/+24 months, delivered energy CAD180/MWh, lost pass-through recovery, interest +200 basis points, and plant replacement/overhaul. Energy pass-through protects the landlord only if the customer can afford and is contractually required to pay it. A combined downside can invalidate a seemingly healthy stabilized cash yield. Do not use terminal value, merchant exports, incentives, heat sales or speculative AI revenues to rescue a weak contracted case.

## 8. Risk register, gates and next decisions

| Decisive risk | Evidence needed | Stop or reshape trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Land/entitlement | Option, title, survey and County interpretation | No controllable/consentable tract by M6 |
| BYOG / grid | Current eligibility, viable studies, costs and operating terms | No written viable route by M12 or credible first service beyond M54 |
| Gas | Firm peak-day delivery and pressure / outage study | Required fuel cannot be secured on bankable terms |
| Receptors / environment | Noise, air, wetland and industrial hazard findings | Material conflict cannot be mitigated within layout and cost |
| Anchor credit / rent | Signed 25 MW take-or-pay and acceptable security | No bankable anchor by M12 at viable economics |
| Supply chain | OEM slots, net guarantees and bounded cancellation exposure | Manufacturing dates or exclusions defeat the delivery case |
| Common-mode outages | Fuel/grid dependency and integrated failure-mode analysis | Customer availability terms cannot be achieved |
| Carbon / levy | Current legal and tax opinion; enforceable customer allocation | Finance-term operating or customer emissions requirements cannot be met |
| Fibre | Physically distinct carrier routes and measured service design | Single shared failure point cannot be addressed economically |
| Financial downside | Updated integrated model against bids and leases | 15% equity screen or lender downside coverage not achieved |

**G0** requires controlled land and a developable-area test. **G1** requires a credible power/fuel route. **G2** requires a consentable layout. **G3** requires bankable first-phase customer and financing terms. **G4** is the investment decision with actual conditions met, funded risk and executable scopes. **G5** is witnessed readiness and customer acceptance. Every gate remains open.

The immediate work is to verify the offering and seller terms; prepare a combined AESO/TFO/generation pre-application package; obtain firm-gas and carrier feasibility; seek County written use classification; commission environmental/geotechnical fatal-flaw work; obtain budgetary equipment scopes; and test tenant pricing/credit against the proposed product. These are a prioritized diligence plan, not actions already performed. A sensible first paid work package would be capped and milestone-based, with title/site, power/gas, environment and customer teams working in parallel before detailed design expands.

# Alberta execution and acceptance package

**13 October 2026 · concept issue · all gates open.** This execution basis accompanies the Alberta dossier, electrical/cooling/layout drawings and executable financial model. It defines what evidence would support a construction and service decision; it does not claim vendor compliance, a booked production slot, an approved operating mode, a lease or an energized site. Project months are conditional planning intervals and carry no calendar-date promise.

The selected design envelope is four 25 MW IT phases, **125 MW campus peak** at an assumed 1.25 peak multiplier, 90 MW ultimate direct-liquid IT heat and 10 MW residual-air IT heat. Ultimate primary generation is **16 × 10 MW net at site**, with cumulative 6 / 9 / 13 / 16 modules for the four phases. With two modules unavailable, those stages provide 40 / 70 / 110 / 140 MW against phase campus peaks 31.25 / 62.5 / 93.75 / 125 MW. This static balance does not prove transient response, gas availability or permissible island operation. Independent emergency diesel remains separate from primary generation.

Physical engine staging and financial cost staging are different. The CAD360m primary-plant allowance places **the full CAD25m gas lateral and CAD30m BESS allowance in phase 1**; the remaining CAD305m is apportioned by 6 / 3 / 4 / 3 additional engines. The gas lateral and complete 25 MW / 25 MWh BESS concept are therefore funded before initial operation, not progressively introduced with the last engines.

| Phase / assumed operation | Added engines / cumulative | Engine-related share of CAD305m | Shared gas lateral + BESS | Allocated plant hard cost |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 / M42 | 6 / 6 | CAD114.375m | CAD55.000m | CAD169.375m |
| 2 / M51 | 3 / 9 | CAD57.1875m | — | CAD57.1875m |
| 3 / M60 | 4 / 13 | CAD76.250m | — | CAD76.250m |
| 4 / M69 | 3 / 16 | CAD57.1875m | — | CAD57.1875m |

The executable model uses those phase cost fractions (approximately 47.0486% / 15.8854% / 21.1806% / 15.8854%) and applies soft cost and contingency separately. Remaining engine balance of plant and dedicated civil/electrical work within CAD305m still follow a proportional approximation; common infrastructure may need further front-loading after a scoped quote. Each phase's allocated cost is spread evenly across its modeled construction interval. Actual supplier deposits, reservation payments, milestone releases and cancellation liabilities are not modeled; a phase-level cost allocation does not prove adequate liquidity on every procurement date.

## Conditions for issuing and releasing procurement

Issue budgetary RFQs during site/power diligence using the same input revision, operating envelope and drawings. Each response must show exclusions, net site ratings, ambient and altitude derating, emissions/noise basis, guaranteed performance, equipment weights/footprints, interface ownership, lead time from an explicit release event, price validity, escalation, cancellation exposure, spare parts, factory testing and on-site support. No response is presumed received.

The M42 first-operation target requires **conditional long-lead release around M8**, because 30 months of manufacture/delivery then runs to M38, leaving approximately four months for final installation, integration and acceptance. A slot reservation that does not start engineering/manufacture is not equivalent to an effective production release. These early commitments would precede some permits and financing conditions. They therefore need explicit sponsor risk approval, capped loss exposure, cancellation/transfer rights where negotiable and sufficient equity; approval in this artifact does not authorize any purchase.

If releases must wait until M24 permit completion, a 30-month package arrives no earlier than about M54 before installation/commissioning. In that case M42 fails and the entire plan and cash model must be rebaselined, provisionally to at least M58 rather than implying vendor acceleration. The executable model presently uses a simplified monthly spend curve and does not represent actual reservation deposits or cancellation liabilities.

| Package | RFQ issue / clarification target | Conditional award or effective release | Site delivery / readiness target | Install and acceptance target | Release evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 240 kV receiving transformers, protection and interconnection engineering | M2–M5 | M8 for 30-month package | M38; foundations/haul route ready earlier | M38–M40 installation; M40–M42 authorized energization and integrated tests | TFO interface accepted; design freeze, access rights, permit/cancellation plan, executable price and manufacture-start obligation |
| First six gas modules and relevant plant balance of plant | M2–M6 | M8 for 30-month package | M38; foundations, gas train and exhaust interfaces ready | M38–M40 erection; M40–M42 plant and campus trials | Net ratings at site; emissions/noise basis; fuel specification and firm service pathway; LTSA and guarantees; acceptable permit exposure |
| Gas lateral, metering, regulation and firm transport | M3–M6 | M12 for 24-month development package | Service-ready target M36, subject to route consents and gas-provider agreement | M36–M40 leak/pressure/control tests and authorized gas-in | Written pressure, capacity, quality and maximum-day duty; easements; upstream interruption terms; no inference from nearby pipe |
| Facility MV/LV, UPS, batteries and emergency diesel | M6–M10 | M16 for 20-month package | M36 | M36–M40 installation; M40–M42 integrated tests | Approved discrimination/grounding basis and IT/cooling ride-through scope; emergency-only operating envelope; rating guarantees |
| BESS, PCS, EMS and plant controller | M6–M10 | M18 for 18-month package | M36 | M36–M40 installation; M40–M42 dynamic tests | 25 MW / 25 MWh remains a placeholder until time-domain study; usable energy, SOC policy, grid-forming need, fire/cyber strategy |
| Liquid cooling, air cooling and dry rejection / trim | M6–M10 | M18 for 18-month package | M36 | M36–M40 hydraulic/electrical work; M40–M42 thermal tests | Tenant water-class and residual-air requirements; site-condition capacity curves; freeze protection and mechanical trim duty |
| Civil works and first hall shell | M8–M12 | M18 enabling scope; field work only after approvals, target M20 | Shell/weather-tight target M34 | M30–M40 phased MEP fit-out overlapping approved areas | Survey, geotechnics, setbacks, drainage, fire access, issued-for-construction drawings and permits |
| Two carrier routes and entries | M4–M8 | M18 for 15-month allowance | M33 service-ready target | M33–M40 independent route tests; M40–M42 tenant acceptance | Carrier route drawings and third-party crossings; confirmed physically separate paths and repair service terms |
| Independent commissioning agent | M6–M9 | M10 design-review appointment | Test procedures and load-bank plan M30–M36 | M36–M42 progressively witnessed completion | Independence, written acceptance criteria, approved safe test modes, calibrated instrumentation and customer/TFO witnesses |

Dates are target gates, not supplier quotes. Later plant stages add **3 engines by M51, 4 by M60 and 3 by M69**. Applying the same 30-month supply plus four-month field-test allowance requires effective releases around **M17, M26 and M35**, respectively. Later release or scope change shifts the corresponding phase; an unexercised framework option is not evidence of manufacturing capacity. Confirmed customer reservations, cancellation security and financing must cover those early expansion commitments. Later civil/MEP execution can overlap operation only with proven physical segregation and approved management of change.

## Commissioning and acceptance matrix

The numeric test durations and excursion envelope below are **proposed contractual acceptance targets**. OEM ratings, tenant tolerance, permits and system-operator requirements may require different tests. Any missing threshold is a hold point for agreeing the protocol, not permission to pass. The independent commissioning authority records procedure revision, prerequisites, calibrated instruments, event/time-series data, defects, retests and signed disposition. Testing that could affect the grid occurs only within authorized switching and operating instructions.

| Test / objective | Proposed measurable acceptance evidence | Witness and hold point |
|---|---|---|
| Equipment and construction completion | 100% of safety-critical punch items closed; approved as-builts, torque/insulation/pressure results, relay settings and cause/effect schedules match installed equipment; no unresolved issue blocks safe isolation | Engineer of record, EPC quality lead and independent commissioning authority; no energization before electrical/gas/fire permissions |
| Net generation rating | Test each engine's net delivered MW at the agreed ambient, altitude, fuel pressure/composition and auxiliary load; contract target 10 MW net/module. Correct to agreed conditions using vendor-approved curves; demonstrate sustained stable operation and record fuel/heat rate/emissions | OEM and independent test engineer; no assumed guarantee from gross nameplate or brochure; site-condition acceptance method agreed before award |
| First phase continuous campus duty | 25 MW metered IT load-bank demand plus measured campus overhead, up to 31.25 MW planning peak, for proposed 24-hour integrated run after thermal stabilization. No unplanned IT power interruption; all agreed electrical and coolant envelopes maintained | Tenant technical representative and commissioning authority; final test load and duration agreed in lease acceptance schedule |
| Ultimate campus duty | Repeat cumulative acceptance at 50/75/100 MW IT, with measured supporting power. Ultimate design envelope 125 MW facility input; at least the proposed 24-hour run at final-stage duty, supported by approved heat-rejection operating conditions | Tenant, EPC and independent authority. Actual IT load/thermal simulators needed; low-load energization is not proof of full duty |
| Primary N+2 static capacity | At each stage demonstrate the full commissioned campus duty with two primary modules unavailable: available design capacity 40/70/110/140 MW. Record every online module's net MW, reserve margin, temperature and fuel conditions | OEM, commissioning authority and operator; this capacity test does not imply tolerance of all common gas/controller faults |
| Dynamic load steps and generator loss | Study and safely test staged ±5 MW IT-equivalent load changes and loss of the largest operating 10 MW generation block as initial planning disturbances; prove bus voltage/frequency and recovery remain inside the **agreed OEM, tenant and operator envelope** with no critical-load dropout | TFO/AESO where applicable, OEM, tenant and commissioning authority; exact ramp, nadir, overshoot and time limits must be signed before acceptance |
| Grid disturbance and separation | If islanding is expressly approved, test authorized utility loss, controlled separation, island stabilization and synchronized reconnection at agreed loading. Capture relay actions, BESS power/SOC, bus quality and IT continuity; no unauthorized backfeed | Utility/system operator and licensed switching authority; approved studies and protection/control settings are prerequisites. If islanding is disallowed, revise the SLA and operating case |
| Black start and emergency recovery | In an approved dead-bus procedure, establish controls, auxiliaries, generation and cooling in the correct sequence, then restore tenant load within the contracted restoration envelope. Demonstrate an independent recovery path when a plant controller or one start source is unavailable | OEM, site operations and commissioning authority; 25 MWh BESS capacity alone does not establish black-start sufficiency |
| IT UPS and cooling/control ride-through | Test one redundant UPS module unavailable while the phase carries 25 MW IT; demonstrate the proposed five-minute IT ride-through using measured delivered battery energy and load. Separately validate control/CDU/pump and residual-air cooling continuity or thermal hold-up during the measured transfer/start interval | Tenant, UPS OEM, cooling OEM and commissioning authority; 8.333 MWh full-campus delivered IT energy is a sizing identity, not an installed battery acceptance certificate |
| Thermal and hydraulic performance | Prove each 25 MW phase rejects 22.5 MW through the direct-liquid path and 2.5 MW through residual-air cooling at assumed 90/10 capture, while total rejection meets measured overhead-inclusive duty. Verify supply/return temperature, flow, differential pressure, water chemistry, leak alarms and balancing; test one cooling/CDU/pump module unavailable | Cooling OEM and tenant; proposed 35/45°C facility loop requires tenant/OEM sign-off. Outdoor design/stress performance requires curves, tests or an agreed seasonal completion plan |
| Freeze and seasonal operation | Validate outdoor fluid freeze protection against agreed −40°C winter screening condition, cold-start and low-load controls, drainage and heat trace; validate +35°C design / +40°C stress screening against site weather basis and net equipment curves | Mechanical engineer and OEM; assumptions are not local design-weather certification or a guarantee that tests occur at those outdoor temperatures |
| Fuel service and safe shutdown | Verify metered pressure/quality/flow across the agreed maximum-day envelope; alarm and safely isolate on gas-quality/pressure excursions; prove gas detection, ventilation, fire interfaces and emergency shutoff | Gas provider, plant OEM, fire/safety authority as applicable; physically separate primary modules do not remove shared upstream-fuel risk |
| Emissions, noise and water compliance | Independent measurements/reports satisfy the actual permit limits and operating restrictions; close all monitoring/reporting prerequisites. Record operational gas and water meters, discharge controls and spill-response equipment | Environmental lead and relevant authority; numeric permit limits must come from the issued approvals, not this concept |
| Facility maintenance and A/B path isolation | Execute agreed maintenance scenarios with safe locked-out equipment while critical loads remain served; trace all shared buses, controls, pipes, fuel and communication paths; document failures outside the maintainability claim | Operator, engineer of record and commissioning authority; module counts alone do not establish a certified topology |
| Network and controls | Trace two off-site routes to independently located carrier infrastructure; prove agreed throughput/latency/failover and alarm delivery. Demonstrate privileged access, backup/restore, time synchronization and OT segmentation without live unauthorized intrusion | Tenant network lead, carriers and controls owner; logical carrier diversity is insufficient if the physical route is shared |
| Operational handover | Approved SOP/MOP/EOP set, asset register, warranty starts, spare inventory, on-call matrix and training records; conduct tabletop plus controlled emergency drills; signed tenant acceptance with only agreed noncritical residual items | Site general manager and tenant; commissioning documents and live staffing must exist before ready-for-service declaration |

## Operating organization and controls

The initial organization is an **indicative staffing plan to cost**, not a claim that the current OPEX allowance has been supported by payroll quotes. A proposed 24/7 core shift comprises a shift lead, a qualified plant/control-room operator, an electrical/critical-facilities technician and a mechanical/cooling technician. Four continuously covered posts require roughly 20–24 trained FTE at a 5–6 FTE relief factor per post, before supervision, dedicated maintenance and security. Professional licensure, power-engineering classification and safe staffing must be confirmed against the selected equipment and applicable Alberta requirements. Do not count an on-call vendor as an on-site shift operator.

| Accountable role | Recurring deliverable and escalation |
|---|---|
| Site general manager | Own service performance, staffing, safety and incident decisions; approve operating readiness and management of change; reconcile budget to the agreed SLA and plant duty |
| Shift lead / control room | 24/7 power, thermal, gas and alarm supervision; signed rounds/logs; dispatch only within the approved import/export and emissions envelope; trigger EOP on threatened limits |
| Electrical lead | Maintain protection settings, battery health, switchgear/transformer condition, isolation permits and switching authority; plan PM windows against live capacity and redundancy |
| Mechanical / cooling lead | Track flow, pressure, chemistry, filters, fluid condition and thermal margins; maintain CDUs/pumps/dry coolers/trim; seasonal freeze and heat-stress readiness |
| Gas-plant lead and LTSA provider | Per-engine run hours/starts, oil analysis, fault trends, OEM bulletins and scheduled overhaul plan; maintain net-rated capacity after planned outages; track exclusions and response commitments |
| Fuel and energy manager | Firm gas nominations/capacity and pressure risk; meter reconciliation, supply/transport terms, cold-day contingency; ensure pass-through bills do not duplicate rent-funded capital or fixed O&M |
| Environmental and safety lead | Permit monitoring, emissions inventory/reporting, noise/water obligations, spill/fire preparedness, contractor controls and regulator notifications under issued conditions |
| Controls / OT and network owner | Access reviews, offline recovery copies, approved patch/testing windows, control-network segmentation, time-series retention and diverse carrier evidence |
| Maintenance planner / stores | CMMS asset register and OEM PM calendar, critical-spare min/max stock, calibration, warranty claims, service bulletins and turnaround logistics |
| Customer service / commercial owner | Capacity and energy billing, SLA/incident reporting, planned-work notices, expansion reservations, credit security and dispute escalation |

Security, HSE, procurement, day maintenance and management are additional costed roles or contracted services. The financial model's fixed OPEX line must be reconciled to this organization and the selected LTSA before underwriting approval. A minimum availability promise cannot rely on staffing or replacement stock that has not been contracted.

The plant LTSA RFQ should define planned service/overhaul intervals, consumables, major component swaps, local response times, guaranteed parts access, performance degradation, fuel exclusions, emissions-system upkeep, liquidated damages and boundaries between warranty, capital overhaul and variable maintenance. Model maintenance capital is a smoothing allowance; it does not place physical spares on site or replace an overhaul cash calendar.

Critical-spares screening includes CDU/pump controls and seals, sensors/meters, valve actuators, protection relays, UPS modules and control boards, battery strings or replacement arrangements, engine ignition/fuel components, filters and fluids, and agreed long-lead transformer/engine exchange strategy. Quantities must follow failure consequence, supplier lead time and actual installed models. Track stock and replenishment; do not assume a spare capacity module contains every replaceable part.

Every intrusive task uses an approved method of procedure with affected load, isolation/lockout, remaining capacity, rollback and witnesses. Major events use immediate safety stabilization, tenant/system-operator/regulator notification according to the actual contracts/permits, preserved time-series/event logs, root-cause review and a tested corrective action. The concept proposes monthly reliability/PM/capacity review and pre-winter/pre-summer readiness reviews; mandatory reporting cadence comes from the final agreements and approvals.

## Anchor-customer term-sheet scope

This is a negotiation checklist and proposed allocation, not a sent offer or legal advice. Counsel must translate it into enforceable facility, energy, easement and intercreditor documents.

| Term | Proposed commercial position / evidence needed |
|---|---|
| Demise and capacity | Initial 25 MW IT block, optionally divisible into 5 MW suites, at a precise IT delivery demarcation; roof/yard, security, service access and fit-out responsibilities explicitly scheduled |
| Rent and duration | Underwriting input CAD235 per committed kW-month; proposed 10–15-year take-or-pay term. It is **not** a cleared price or proof the 15% hurdle is met. Reprice against the live model and lender requirements before FID |
| Metered power | Pass actual agreed variable operating energy cost through separately; define meters, losses/PUE allocation, audit rights, imbalance/demand costs, gas/carbon exposure, taxes and dispute mechanism. No hidden second recovery of owner-financed generation capital |
| Indexation and costs | Negotiate indexed rent and OPEX treatment; executable base model assumes zero escalation. Explicitly allocate equipment levy, tax changes and carbon costs; no tax-credit realization assumed |
| Tenant interfaces | Rack loading/density, cooling class/chemistry/flow/pressure, water ownership, residual-air load, voltage/quality, dynamic load changes, firmware/control compatibility and fiber requirements confirmed before design freeze |
| Ready for service | Tied to signed acceptance protocol and permits, not a utility energization notice alone. Phase-specific long-stop, tenant access, test loads, punch-list handling and early-access liability negotiated |
| Availability and curtailment | SLA based on approved and tested topology and fuel/grid modes; specify planned maintenance, lawful curtailment, tenant load-step limits and service credits. Do not promise off-grid independence before approved island tests |
| Security and remedies | Credit-approved parent guarantee, cash security or LC; capped delay/service remedies, termination and cure rights; lender direct agreement and step-in rights negotiated without assuming bankability |
| Expansion | Separate, time-limited and funded options for later 25 MW phases; reservation deadlines aligned with engine manufacture releases and tenant cancellation exposure; avoid building speculative phases on nonbinding interest |
| Data and sustainability | Customer data-residency/security obligations distinct from facility marketing; disclose gas generation, emissions calculation boundary and renewable claims only to the extent contractually evidenced |
| Acceptance of economics | Current base-case returns and terminal debt obligations supplied with the term sheet; if lease price or risk allocation fails underwriting, reopen economics rather than describe a conditional customer as committed |

## Current open evidence

Before a financed notice to proceed, obtain the actual site survey and usable acreage, approved BYOG/grid operating envelope, gas service agreement, applicable planning/environmental/plant approvals, signed OEM performance/lead-time/LTSA terms, constructible coordinated design, tenant technical schedule and credit-backed lease, independently reconciled budget/contingency, staffing and overhaul plan, and lender-approved funding/covenants. All remain open. The proposal is complete as a development concept only; external readiness requires these documents and witnessed results.

## Model qualifications

- Concept estimates, not contractor quotes, grid rights, permit approvals or a financing offer.
- Pre-tax, constant nominal inputs: no inflation/escalation, corporate/income tax, depreciation, grants, terminal asset value or GPU purchases.
- PUE is an annual input, not an hourly weather simulation; low-load fixed power and demand ratchets are not modeled.
- Electricity is passed through at cost; changes affect tenant cost, not landlord EBITDA. Owned-plant energy price must contain variable generation costs only.
- No lease ramp: each commissioned phase immediately reaches the chosen occupancy. Schedule is conditional, not a forecast of approval.
- Returns use monthly timing; annual DSCR uses cash available after maintenance capital, including any final debt balloon.
- Debt extends beyond the project horizon: the final cash flow includes repayment of the remaining principal.
- Primary generation plant is separately owned in this scenario. Its fixed O&M must be included in fixed OPEX; major overhauls and fuel/carbon exposure require dedicated diligence.
- Pre-tax, un-escalated planning model; no depreciation, income tax, incentives or GPU assets.
- No terminal sale proceeds or land salvage; utility collateral returns at the modeled horizon.
- No lease-up ramp: occupancy applies from each phase commissioning date.
- Maintenance reserve is preliminary; plant major overhauls and tenant equipment levy require separate diligence.
